trap: The five small parables get flattened into "the kingdom is great, so try hard" — losing both the joy (the man sells all gladly, not grimly) and the realism (the net holds bad fish too). Or only the comfortable images get preached and the net's hard sorting quietly drops out.
hinge: The treasure costs everything and is stumbled on by accident, bought with joy; the leaven is hidden and tiny yet takes over the whole; the net gathers everyone yet sorts at the shore. Free gift and total cost, smallest and total, gathered and sifted — all at once.

doors.claim: The kingdom starts as the smallest, most hidden thing and works silently through the whole — so do not despise small beginnings, and let grace leaven all of you.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: The leaven signifies love, because it causes activity and fermentation; the love implanted in us ought to grow until it changes the whole soul into its own perfection.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: The Lord compares himself to leaven, for leaven communicates the power it has received to a whole heap of its own kind.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: So long ought charity, hidden in the mind, to grow, until it change the whole mind into its own perfection, so that it love or think upon nothing beside God, which is begun here, and perfected in the other life.

doors.say: What God has hidden in you is small and quiet now, but it is meant to work through the whole of your life.
doors.do: Point to one hidden, unglamorous beginning of grace in them, and have them let it spread to one more corner this week.

doors.claim: The one who finds the treasure and the pearl sells everything — not grimly but gladly — because next to the one thing, everything else is worth letting go.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: The pearl of great price is the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, which he who has found it sells all and buys.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: He hides the treasure not out of envy, but as one who treasures up what he would not lose — he hides in his heart the thing he prizes.

doors.say: When you have really seen the treasure, letting the rest go stops feeling like loss and starts feeling like joy.
doors.do: Name one thing they are clutching that is keeping their hands too full to take the pearl — and invite them to sell it, gladly.

doors.claim: The net gathers every kind of fish, and the sorting comes only at the shore — so being inside the catch is not yet being safe; do not presume.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: When the net is drawn to the shore, then will be shown the true test for separating the fishes.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Lest we trust in preaching only, or think faith enough by itself without a life, he adds the net: good and bad are gathered, and parted only at the end.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The Gospel, wherever it is preached, gathers at first both good and bad, who are for a season full of approbation and warm with good desires. But Christian discipline, and strong, close exhortation, begin that separation in this world, which shall be accomplished by the angels of God in the world to come.

doors.say: You are in the net — gathered, named, carried — and the net is not yet the shore; live like it.
doors.do: Turn presumption into watchfulness: one way the hearer has mistaken being gathered for being finished.

complementary.gravity: Solomon, offered anything at all, asks not for riches but for an understanding heart; Paul declares that nothing can separate us from the love of God; and Jesus piles up images of a kingdom worth selling everything to own. The nerve: what is the one thing you would trade all the others for — and have you found it?

synthesis.convergence: Each text turns on valuing the one thing: Solomon asking for an understanding heart instead of riches (1 Kings 3), the psalmist prizing God's word above gold (Psalm 119), Paul certain that nothing is worth being cut off from God's love (Romans 8), and a kingdom worth selling everything to own (the parables).
synthesis.claim: There is one thing worth more than all the rest, and it has already found you — sell everything, and keep it gladly.
synthesis.here: For people whose lives are cluttered with many goods and many worries, the move is to name the single treasure and let everything else find its true size — resting, with Paul, in the truth that the treasure (God's love) is holding them, not the other way around.

doors.landing: Seven years like a few days
doors.claim: Jacob's love makes the long labor light: what we give ourselves to out of love does not feel like a sentence.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: They seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her — an age of work will be but as a few days to those that love God, and long for Christ's appearing.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: How was this said, since even a short time seems long to them that love? It was said therefore because of the labour of the servitude, which love made easy.

doors.say: Seven years of hard work, and Jacob said it felt like a few days. Love does that to time.
doors.do: Ask them where their faith has become a sentence to serve, and what it would take to love their way back into it.

doors.claim: Jacob, who tricked his father in the dark, is tricked in the dark himself: the story lets his own deceit come home to him.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Jacob had cheated his own father when he pretended to be Esau, and now his father-in-law cheated him. Herein, how unrighteous soever Laban was, the Lord was righteous.

doors.say: The man who pretended to be his brother woke up married to the wrong sister. What we do to others has a way of finding us.
doors.do: Invite them to name one deception they have practiced and have not yet set right, and to take one step toward setting it right.

semicontinuous.gravity: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, and they seem to him but a few days for the love he has for her; then the deceiver is deceived and wakes beside Leah (Genesis 29). The Psalm calls Israel to remember the covenant God keeps for a thousand generations; Paul is sure nothing can separate us from God's love (Romans 8); and Jesus tells of a man who sells everything for one treasure. The nerve: what love will pay, and the faithfulness of God that holds even through our tangled bargains.

synthesis.convergence: Jacob gives seven years for Rachel and counts them a few days, only to have his bargain turned back on him (Genesis 29); the Psalm remembers a covenant God keeps across a thousand generations (Psalm 105); Paul is persuaded nothing can separate us from the love of God (Romans 8); and the kingdom is a treasure worth selling everything for (Matthew 13). The readings set the costly love we give beside the steadier love God keeps, even when our own dealings go crooked.
synthesis.claim: Love makes long service short, and God's faithfulness runs underneath even the bargains that go wrong.
synthesis.here: For people who gave years to something and feel cheated by how it turned out, the move is to hear that those years were not lost on God, who stays faithful when Laban does not, and when we do not.

subtract: Three doors, three landings — transformation (hidden leaven), joyful surrender (sell all), sober self-examination (the net and the shore). Choose one and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
